text: Pepi Litman (Yiddish: פּעפּי ליטמאַן, born Pesha Kahane; c. 1876 – 13 September 1930) was a cross-dressing female Yiddish vaudeville singer associated with the Broderzinger movement. She led a popular traveling theater troupe across Europe, performing highly satirical songs while costumed as a male Hasidic Jew, and is considered a proto-drag king performer due to her frequent performances as a young boy or male dandy. Litman made numerous 78rpm recordings that capture her energetic and virtuosic singing style and serve as a document of Jewish life in Eastern Europe. Born to poor Jewish parents in Tarnopol, a city in eastern Galicia (now in Ukraine), she grew up in a region that was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, where Jews were relatively free to work and travel. However, a poor Jewish girl with no dowry faced very limited prospects in nineteenth-century Eastern Europe, typically working uncompensated throughout her life to support her parents, husband, children, and in-laws. In her youth, she worked as a maid in a theatrical boarding house run by the parents of Max Badin, an actor who later appeared in American Yiddish films, and soon became involved with the itinerant Yiddish vaudevillians known as the Broderzingers. The Broderzingers are credited with creating the earliest form of secular Yiddish theater in East European pubs, cafes, and wine gardens, combining elements of the traditional rabbinical court jester, the badkhn (master of ceremonies at a Yiddish wedding), and the Purimshpil (traditional holiday plays, usually performed privately by amateurs, with cross-dressing, satire, and bawdy songs). Influenced by the Jewish Enlightenment, or Haskalah, the Broderzingers advocated for modernization, education, and emancipation for Jews, and their songs sometimes satirized Hasidism or were sung from the perspective of working-class proste yidn (Yiddish: simple folk) such as nightwatchmen, water carriers, gravediggers, housemaids, and beggars. Pepi married Jacob Litman or Littman, a bandleader and Broderzinger who ran his own traveling theater troupe; after his death, she took over the troupe and toured inns, small towns, health spas, cities, and private homes in Russia, Poland, Germany, Austria, Hungary, and Rumania. According to eyewitness accounts cited by Zalmen Zylbercweig's Leksikon fun Yidishn Teater (Lexicon of the Yiddish Theatre), Litman spoke several languages, frequented literary Yiddish circles, and observed Jewish law as much as possible on the road by keeping kosher and lighting Shabes candles. Jacob Mestel, a co-editor of the Leksikon, called her "a chansonette in Hasidic trousers." Zylbercweig quotes another eyewitness account describing her as dressed in a Hasidic outfit—wearing a big fur hat, curly peyes framing her round, full feminine face, a wide unbuttoned coat with short trousers, white socks, and pumps, with her hands twirling her peyes—bursting from behind the curtains to sing, instantly captivating the audience, both on the floor and in the balconies, as people of all classes sang along. Pepi Litman had a masculine voice, deep and hoarse, but anyone who once heard her sing "Yismekhu" could never forget it. In 1910, journalist M. J. Landa reviewed her performance in Lemberg, Poland, as part of a "Zydowska Kabaretu" [Polish: "Jewish Cabaret"], writing that she was the "star" of the program, and that the moment she stepped on stage dressed as a Galician youth with a skull cap and ringlets, the room's atmosphere changed. He praised her voice as a rich, clear mezzo of operatic fullness and breadth, with moments that were thrilling and others that sounded harsh during repartee with the audience. He noted her banters and expostulations were always good-humored and that she shared the same delight in singing and patter as her audience. He described her as the incarnation of the joyous spirit of the Jew, with moments of pathos and sentiment, and stated that listening to her songs "Shabbos After Table," "Kol Yisrael Chaverim," and an amusing ditty about the Messiah coming in an automobile made him forget the poverty he had experienced in Galicia. From about 1905 to 1930, Litman performed in Germany (especially in spa towns like Marienbad and Karlsbad), Hungary (in Budapest), Poland (especially in Lemberg/Lviv), Russia (especially in Odessa), and likely in America, as she recorded several 78RPM discs in New York. She performed both comic and serious songs in a broad Galitsyaner Yiddish dialect, sometimes in a Germanized form of Yiddish called daytshmerish, and recorded songs in Lemberg, Budapest, and New York. She also worked closely with Broderzinger author and composer Shloyme Pryzament. During World War I, she primarily performed in and around Odessa, where she gained a following in literary circles and was frequently a guest of Yiddish writer and editor David Frishman and author Mendele Mocher Sforim. She returned to performing in Vienna in 1928, touring through Karlsbad, Marienbad, and Poland. After becoming quite ill following this tour, she stayed at the Rothschild Hospital and died on 13 September 1930. Her funeral was arranged by the Vienna Yiddish Artists Union and her burial plot was donated by the Jewish community.
